div.head: 1: Introduction
div.p: In March of 1999, the Object Management Group (OMG) put out a request for proposals (RFP) seeking a standard way of modeling real-time systems using its Unified Modeling Language (UML) [24]. Specifically, this RFP sought a UML profile' for modeling time and timing mechanisms so that models developed under that profile could be analyzed using standard schedulability afid performance ana! ysis techniques [23].

A consortium of real-time tool vendors responded to this RFP with a joint submission in July of 2000 (NB: there were no other competing submissions) [25]. The default OMG process calls for a public review of initial submissions. Based on the feedback resulting from this review, a revised submission is then prepared and, presuming an affirmative vote by the OMG membership, it is adopted as an official OMG technology recommendation. For the realtime profile, the projected date of the revised submission is June of 2001.

As noted, the success of the revision is critically dependent on adequate public feedback to the initial submission. Therefore, the primary purpose of this invited paper is to familiarize the broader community of real-time experts I . A UML profile is a set of extensions to the standard UML that refines certain general UML concepts to more accurately represent the specifics of a given domain or application. This is achieved using the built-in e.uet1sibiliry ttiechonistm of UML (stereotypes, tagged values and constraints).

(i.e., beyond just the OMG membership) with the initial submission and to solicit constructive feedback that can then be incorporated into the revised submission. Of course, given the usual size limitations imposed on conference papers, this paper can only provide a high-level overview. For more details, readers need to refer to the actual submission document [25].

Much has already been written on the topic of applying UML to real-time problems and whether and how it needs to be extended for this purpose ([21 1.51 [81 [91 [ill [I21 [I51 [I71 [18] [26] [28] [30] [31]). The authors of the proposed real-time profile have taken into account this body of work as well as other work dealing with object-oriented real-time systems ([ 11 [20]) and have incorporated much of it into their proposal.

We first examine the objectives of the standard and then the salient features of the approach taken in the initial sub- mission. This is followed by a description of the conceptual foundation, or reference model, that is the basis for this profile and possibly some future real-time profiles. This model is then used for representing different models of time and timing mechanisms, which is described in section 4. The key "sub-profile" for schedulability analysis, also based on the same reference model, is reviewed in section 5. The paper closes with an outline of current plans for the revised submission as well as other real-time modeling standards work within the OMG.

div.head: 2: Objectives and Approach
div.p: A principal objective of the RFP was to allow the construction of predictive UML models, that is, models that can be used to compute key system properties-such as responsiveness, schedulability, and resource requirementsbefore the system is actually constructed. This means providing modelers with the capability to attach quantitative information to a UML model in standard ways so that it can be shared between model editing tools and model anal-ysis tools.

In addition, the RFP suggests that the process of analyzing such models should be automatable. The process envisaged behind this requirement is depicted in Figure 1: The modeler constructs a UML model that includes supplementary annotations required by different kinds of model processors. (Note that the same model may be analyzed from multiple different viewpoints. Furthermore, some tools may even automatically synthesize parts of the userdefined model thereby ensuring optimality of the design.) The annotated model is then transferred to the model processing tools where it is analyzed (or synthesized) and the results fed back to the model editor. Since the annotations are based on a standard, it is possible to combine different tools from different vendors.

Each analysis tool automatically transforms the UML model into the internal form required by its analysis method. Consequently, the details of analysis algorithms and data representations remain hidden from the modeler who does not have to be a domain expert to take advantage of the analysis. This is quite important, since the technical intricacy of current analysis methods has been one of the biggest impediments to their more widespread use in practice.
Figure 1. The model processing paradigm
In response to these and other objectives of the RFP, the approach taken was guided by the following foundational design principles:

Modelers should not be hindered in the way they use UML to represent their systems. That is, rather than enforcing a specific approach or modeling style for real-time systems, the profile should allow modelers to choose the style and modeling constructs that they feel are the best fit to their needs and preferences.

It must be possible to construct UML models that can be used to analyze and predict the salient realtime properties of a system. In particular, it is important to be able to perform such analyses early in the development cycle.

Modelers should be able to take advantage of different types of analysis techniques without requiring indepth understanding of those techniques. In addition to supporting current mainstream real-time technologies, design paradigms, and analysis techniques, the profile should also be fully open to supporting new developments in these areas.

These design principles resulted in a profile that is structured as shown by the UML diagram in Figure 2. The shaded packages are the portions that were actually defined in the initial submission, and the unshaded ones are those that are planned to be added in the final revised submission. The packages drawn using dashed lines represent potential custom or standard extensions.

The Common Base package contains several frameworks that cover aspects that are essential to practically all real-time systems. At its core is a reference model for modeling different kinds of resources. In particular, this includes support for the notion of quality of service (QoS), which is the basis for all quantitative information used in either analysis or synthesis. Two additional foundational frameworks, one for modeling time and another for modeling concurrency, are derived directly from that reference model.

This base is used to define two different categories of sub-profiles. The analysis (and synthesis) sub-profiles are intended for different kinds of analysis (or synthesis) methods. The initial submission only defines a sub-profile for schedulability analysis, but additional ones can be defined for other kinds of time-based analyses or as alternatives to the ones that already exist. It is even possible to further refine these analysis sub-profiles to create more specialized versions. These may or may not be standardized.

The second category of profiles consists of modeling support for specific technologies, such as Real-Time CORBA, the real-time model of CORBA timing services [21][22], or profiles for individual real-time operating systems published by real-time technology vendors. This is similar in concept and intent to the VHDL specifications that hardware vendors publish with their components. Such profile libraries could be used to analyze systems that are based on those specific technologies.

div.head: 3: The Conceptual Foundation: Modeling Resources
div.p: A salient characteristic of most real-time software is that both its physical and its logical aspects are important. While the logical part of the specification determines a system's operational (functional) correctness, the physical properties can have an equally significant impact on its validity. This is because real-time systems have definite quantitative constraints, such as response time requirements, which are ultimately dependent on the physical attributes of the underlying implementation technologies.

The physical aspect of software is traditionally represented through the notion of a resource. It reflects, either directly or indirectly, the finite nature of the underlying environment. Note that resources in software systems do not necessarily have to be physical devices. In addition to components such as processors and networks, the concept encompasses logical devices such as buffers and virtual circuits. However, there is always some physical underpinning to every logical device.

In our model, a resource is viewed as a server that provides one or more services to its clients. The physical limitations of a resource are represented through its quality of service attributes (or, QoS attributes for short). In general, QoS attributes characterize how well a resource service is performed.

QoS attributes can be used to model many different properties. They are mostly quantitative (e.g., size, service time, capacity), but may also be qualitative specifications that ultimately have some quantitative impact (e.g., a scheduling policy or failure model).

Understanding the relationship between a resource and its clients is fundamental in any quantitative analysis technique. Of course, it is not sufficient to know only what QoS a resource can offer, but also what its clients demand. This suggests differentiating the notions of oJjrered QoS (on the resource side) and required QoS (on the client side). Quantitative analyses of shared resource systems can involve some very sophisticated techniques such as schedulability analysis or queueing theory; but, in the end, they all boil down to a comparison of these two sides of the QoS relationship to determine whether the supply can meet the demand.

Most analysis and synthesis methods operate over specific cases, representing either typical or exceptional situations that are of concern to the analyst. We refer to a situation involving resources and their clients as an analysis contexf. This context may be static, consisting simply of a configuration of resources and their clients, or it may be dynamic. In the dynamic case, the load on the resources is represented by dynamic behavioral patterns (e.g., using UML collaborations) of clients using resources. These UML model in Figure 3 shows these fundamental notions and the relationships between them. This reference model is the basis for all other aspects of the real-time UML profile and is referred to as the general model of resource usage, or simply as the general resource model. All dynamic analysis methods rely on the notion of a dynamic scenario, which usually represents a prototypical execution of the system. In our model, a scenario consists of a causally ordered set of scenario steps that represent different activities required in the scenario. Some of these activities may involve interactions between clients and resources. These interactions are represented by scenario events. An event may target one or more resources, or, in more refined models, it may be directed at specific resource services.
In turn, a service (or a resource) may respond to an invocation by initiating its own scenario execution. This provides the option of modeling nested invocations.

The general resource model shown in Figure 3 is a domain model that provides a basis for defining appropriate extensions to UML. The concepts of that model are typically captured with corresponding stereotypes and tagged values. Due to space limitations, we will not go into the details of these the actual extensions. The roots of the stereotype hierarchy are shown in Figure 5. A common stereotype, GRMstereotype, is defined that serves as the root of all stereotypes associated with the general resource model. This simplifies detection of such stereotypes by analysis tools. Note that GRMstereotype is a stereotype of the UML concept called ModelElement, which is the root element of practically all UML concepts.

This allows a stereotype to be associated with different kinds of UML concepts. While this sounds like it is too flexible, it is necessary since we often need to attach the same stereotype to either a class specification or a specification of an instance of that class (these are different base concepts in the UML metamodel). To prevent real-time stereotypes from being associated with arbitrary elements, each stereotype has additional constraints that restrict it to only a subset of possible metamodel elements.

The object diagram in Figure 6, is an example of a simple static analysis context in which the services used by the clients are not modeled explicitly. It shows two active and potentially concurrent clients accessing a shared monitor resource. The QoS char-acteristics are shown as tagged values within the corresponding model elements. This example also illustrates the value of including QoS characteristics in the model. We can immediately identify, without resorting to a sophisticated analysis, that the nominal response time offered by the monitor (4 milliseconds) is insufficient to satisfy the deadlines imposed by the client. (Note that it may be insufficient for the second client as well. However, that cannot be determined until other factors, such as other objects sharing the same CPU, are taken into account.)

div.head: 4: Modeling Time
div.p: The UML standard does not impose any restrictions on the modeling of time. It neither assumes that time is discrete or continuous, nor does it assume that there is a single source of time values in a system. This semantic flexibility allows different representations of time. We retain this flexibility in the proposed profile.
The general model of time and timing mechanisms of the real-time profile is shown in the diagram in Figure 7.

As discussed previously, it is a derivative of the general resource model. (NB: most of the material for this section was derived from the works of Motus [19] and Kopetz [14]; as well as several other related standards [7][10].) Physical time is generally modeled as a set of physical time instants, as perceived by some observer, such that it is a fully ordered set, which means that, for any two distinct elements of the set, p and q, either p precedes q, or q precedes p it is a dense set, which is to say that there is always at least one instant between any pair of instants Since physical time is incorporeal, we typically measure its progress by counting the number of expired cycles of some strictly periodic reference clock' starting from some origin. This way of measuring time necessarily results in a discretization effect in which multiple physical instants are associated with the same count. However, this is merely a consequence of the measurement method and not an inherent property of physical time. In other words, we can obtain whatever time resolution we need simply by choosing a sufficiently short cycle time (resolution) for our reference clock.

The count associated with a particular instant is called its timestamp. In our general model, a timestamp is an instance of an abstract data type called time value. Time values can be represented by simple integers (discrete time values) or by real numbers (dense time values), as well as more sophisticated structured data types such as dates or clock values.

Each concrete time value representation has its own idiosyncratic arithmetic rules, but they all support at least the following meaningful operations on time values (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and comparison).

Events are assumed to occur instantaneously in the sense that they happen at particular time instants and have no duration. A special kind of event is a time event. The occurrence of a time event means that a particular instant in time has been reached. This may be due to the expiry of some interval (i.e., a time-out) or the occurrence of a par-1. For simplicity, we assume that the reference process is co-located with the observer (negligible observation delay). ticular date or absolute clock reading. Time events are generated by timers (described below).
There are two basic types of timing mechanisms: timers and clocks. Both clocks and timers are examples of resources as defined in the generic resource model.

Clocks are mechanisms that periodically generate special kinds of time events called clock ticks. They have standard operations that allow them to be set to a given value, to be read, stopped (which suspends the generation of clock ticks), and started (which resumes the generation of clock ticks). At any point in time, a clock has a current time value that represents the total amount of time that the clock has been running (i.e., generating clock ticks) since its origin. The origin represents a time instant from which the clock measures time. If the clock has never been stopped since the origin and has not exceeded its maximal time, then the current value of the clock will represent the duration between the origin and the present. If the clock has been stopped or stopped and resumed one or more times, then its current value will be reduced by the cumulative duration of the intervals during which it was not running. The maximal value of a clock is simply the highest time value that the clock can represent. After that it may wrap around or remain stopped.

A clock has a number of important offered QoS characteristics. All of these are expressed in terms of a "reference" or standard clock, which is normally some kind of ideal clock, such as a clock maintained by an international standards organization. It is generally desirable to keep a clock as closely synchronized with its reference clock as possible. The offset characteristic of a clock at some instant is the absolute time difference between the time of its clock tick and the corresponding tick of its reference clock. The accuracy of a clock represents the maximum offset of a clock over time. Drift represents the maximum absolute difference in the relative frequencies of the clock and its reference clock between two successive ticks. Finally, the granukari9 of a clock is the duration (measured in terms of the reference clock) between two successive ticks.

A timer is a mechanism for generating timeout events when a particular time instant has occurred. The value of a timer represents the duration that must expire before the timeout event occurs. This means that a timer is always associated with a particular clock and, therefore, assumes the offered QoS characteristics of that clock. Like clocks, timers may be started and stopped and their value read and changed. However, in contrast to clocks, timers are dynamic entities that can also be destroyed when they are no longer needed. If a timer is running when it is destroyed, the effect is that of stopping the timer permanently.

Timers will generate a single timeout event when their duration expires, unless they are periodic. Periodic timers are timers that act like clocks (except that they generate timeout events instead of clock ticks), whose resolution is equal to the value of the timer.

div.head: 5: Schedulability Analysis Models
div.p: Schedulability analysis refers to the set of techniques that are used to determine whether a given configuration of software and hardware is "schedulable", that is, whether it will meet its specified deadlines or not. This field is quite active as a number of useful schedulability analysis techniques have evolved [4][13][16][20] and new ones are steadily emerging [6].

The schedulability analysis profile is derived from the general resource model as shown in Figure 8. It defines a set of specializations of the concepts from that reference model, which explicitly identify a set of QoS characteristics that are used by common schedulability analysis techniques.

Figure 8. The schedulability analysis model A real-time situation is a specific kind of analysis context that consists of a set of resources and a set of schedulable entities. The latter are specializations of resource usage scenarios. They specify causally chained sequences of action specifications (resource actions) that utilize resources (accessed resources). These specifications are executed in a series of steps performed by one or more processing resources and result in a series of events that induce subsequent steps.

div.head: 6: Future Work
div.p: It is currently anticipated that the final submission will incorporate the following additional profile elements:

A general model of concurrency and concurrency management mechanisms (taskdthreads, scheduling contexts, schedulers, etc.). This model will also be based on the general resource model. An additional analysis sub-profile for concepts used in common performance modeling techniques based on queueing theory [ 12][32].

A standard model library and a possible set of extensions for Real-Time CORBA and for the CORBA Enhanced Timing Service. In addition to this real-time profile the OMG is working on defining requirements for additional profiles related to real-time systems. The next RFP will most likely focus on the ability to model other QoS characteristics that are not related directly to time (e.g., availability, reliability, safety). The authors of the current initial submission had this in view and defined the general resource model in such a way that it will likely provide the necessary conceptual underpinning for this as well. Finally, a third RFP is also planned to address the issues pertaining to modeling of the architectures of complex real-time systems.
